topics.description: A virtual network: an isolated, software-defined network within a provider's infrastructure, where you choose your own private address ranges and subnets instead of sharing the provider's default network. AWS calls this a VPC, Azure a Virtual Network, and Google Cloud a VPC network — different names for the same isolation model, which is what the exam cares about.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: A subdivision of a virtual network (AWS's VPC, Azure's Virtual Network, Google Cloud's VPC network) that carves out part of its address range for a group of resources. Its relationship to availability zones differs by provider: on AWS, a subnet is confined to a single Availability Zone, so a multi-AZ design needs one subnet per zone. On Azure and Google Cloud, a subnet is not zone-scoped — an Azure virtual network and its subnets span every availability zone in the region, and a Google Cloud subnet is a regional resource that can hold instances across multiple zones in its region at once. "Subnet" itself is the same term everywhere; the zone-scoping is the AWS-specific detail, not a shared rule.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: A public subnet has a route to an internet gateway and so can be reached from, and reach, the internet directly; a private subnet has no such route and can only initiate outbound connections indirectly, through NAT. Whether a subnet is "public" or "private" is a property of its route table, not of the subnet itself — adding the route is what makes it public.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: Two layers of cloud network filtering. A security group is a stateful firewall attached to an individual resource: allow an inbound request and the matching outbound reply is allowed back automatically. A network access control list (network ACL) is stateless and attaches to a subnet instead, so inbound and outbound rules must each be written explicitly. AWS names both this way; Azure's Network Security Groups are stateful with no separate stateless layer, and Google Cloud's VPC firewall rules are likewise stateful and apply network-wide rather than per subnet. The stateful/instance-level versus stateless/subnet-level split is the exam-relevant idea, not the AWS names for it.
topics.notes: The stateful/stateless difference is the crux and is easy to get backwards. Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: Two routing targets with opposite reachability. Routing a subnet's traffic through an internet gateway gives it two-way internet reachability, so it can be reached from outside. AWS's internet gateway is a resource you explicitly create and attach to a VPC; Google Cloud's routing documentation names the same role a "default internet gateway," the next hop of its system-generated default route, though it is not something you provision the way an AWS internet gateway is; Azure has no separately named equivalent resource for inbound reachability; outbound reachability used to be an inherent, unrouted property of a virtual network, but the Azure portal already defaults new subnets to private, and in the API version released after 2026-03-31 that becomes the default everywhere (ARM templates, PowerShell, and CLI too) — so an explicit outbound method is now required rather than assumed. Routing traffic instead through a NAT gateway (also offered as Azure NAT Gateway and Google Cloud's Cloud NAT) allows outbound-only connections: private resources can reach out but cannot be reached from outside. The direction of reachability is what an exam question turns on, not the resource names.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: A publicly routable address assigned to a cloud resource. By default such addresses are ephemeral, released back to the provider's pool when the resource is deleted; a static, reserved version instead survives instance replacement and can be remapped to a new instance without updating DNS. AWS calls its reserved version an Elastic IP, Azure a static public IP, and Google Cloud a static external IP address — the reserved-versus-ephemeral distinction is the same everywhere.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: A managed, authoritative DNS service run by the cloud provider, often integrated with its load balancers and health checks so DNS answers can change automatically on a failure (DNS failover). AWS's version is Route 53, Azure's is Azure DNS, and Google Cloud's is Cloud DNS — the DNS-plus-health-check integration is the exam-relevant behavior, not any one product name.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: A layer 4 (transport-layer) load balancer forwards connections by address and port alone, blind to the application protocol. A layer 7 (application-layer) load balancer reads the request itself and can route on details like hostname or URL path. AWS offers these as its Network Load Balancer and Application Load Balancer, Azure as Load Balancer and Application Gateway, and Google Cloud as its Network and HTTP(S) Load Balancers — different names for the same layer-4-versus-layer-7 split.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Connecting two networks privately at the IP level, without traversing the public internet — whether that is two virtual networks within the same provider, or (see hybrid connectivity) a cloud network and an on-premises site. AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud all call the cloud-to-cloud case "peering" (VPC Peering, VNet Peering, and VPC Network Peering respectively): traffic stays on the provider's private backbone instead of routing over the internet.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: Joining an on-premises network to a cloud network either over a VPN tunnel across the public internet, or via a dedicated private circuit that bypasses the internet for more predictable bandwidth and latency. AWS's dedicated-circuit product is Direct Connect, Azure's is ExpressRoute, and Google Cloud's is Interconnect. The VPN-versus-dedicated-circuit trade-off — cost and setup time against performance and reliability — is what an exam question turns on.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: either end of a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: Rules that determine where traffic leaving a subnet is sent next, keyed by destination address range. Associating a subnet with a route table that includes a route to an internet gateway is what actually makes that subnet "public" — the subnet carries no flag saying so itself. AWS and Azure both call this a route table associated per subnet; Google Cloud instead defines routes at the network level, matched by destination and instance tag, but the underlying job — choosing a packet's next hop — is the same.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: A single hardened, audited host that administrators connect to first and hop from to reach private resources, so those resources need no direct inbound exposure of their own. Traditionally a self-managed jump box, this is increasingly a managed service instead — Azure Bastion, Google Cloud's Identity-Aware Proxy, or AWS Systems Manager Session Manager — which removes the need to expose SSH or RDP to the internet at all.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Choosing non-overlapping private address ranges (CIDR blocks) for each virtual network up front. Two networks with overlapping ranges cannot be peered or privately connected without re-addressing. The range is not actually locked at creation on any of the three major providers — AWS supports associating additional (secondary) CIDR blocks with an existing VPC, Google Cloud supports expanding a subnet's primary IPv4 range in place, and Azure supports adding address space to an existing virtual network — but none of that helps once other subnets, peering connections, or on-premises routes are already built around the original range: growing addressable space is comparatively easy, undoing an overlap is not. That asymmetry is why the initial choice still has to be made carefully, not because it can never change.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Reaching a managed provider service — object storage, a managed database, a queue — over the provider's private network rather than routing out to the public internet, improving both security and egress cost. AWS's version is PrivateLink, Azure's is Private Link, and Google Cloud's is Private Service Connect: functionally equivalent private-endpoint mechanisms under three different names.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.
